content: Under Regulation E, the institution must provisionally credit the consumer's account within 10 business days if the investigation is not complete, unless a written confirmation is provided within the timeframe.
The institution shall complete its investigation within 45 calendar days (90 for new accounts or POS/foreign transactions) of receiving notice of error.
Access to nonpublic personal information must follow least-privilege principles; analysts may access only records within their assigned dispute class.
Type A disputes concern unauthorized or fraudulent card use. Type B disputes concern merchant or quality issues. Analysts are credentialed to one class.
All access to customer dispute records must be logged with actor, scope, resource, and decision, and retained for audit.
Upon receiving an oral or written notice of error, the institution must investigate and determine whether an error occurred within the prescribed timeframe and report the results to the consumer.
Consumer liability for unauthorized electronic fund transfers is capped at $50 if reported within two business days, and $500 thereafter, provided notice is given within 60 days of the statement.
If the investigation determines no error occurred, any provisional credit may be reversed after providing the consumer five business days' written notice and honoring transactions for that period.
On request, the consumer is entitled to copies of the documents the institution relied on in its error determination, furnished promptly and without charge.
Provisional credit applies when an investigation extends beyond ten business days and the consumer has provided timely notice of the disputed electronic fund transfer.
The provisional credit equals the disputed transaction amount plus any associated fees or interest assessed as a result of the alleged error.
Provisional credit must post to the available balance no later than the close of the tenth business day so the consumer has full use of the funds during the investigation.
The institution maintains a written information security program with administrative, technical, and physical safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of customer information.
Third-party service providers handling nonpublic personal information must be contractually bound to implement and maintain equivalent safeguards, with periodic assessment.
Suspected unauthorized access to customer information triggers the incident response plan, including containment, investigation, regulatory notification, and customer notice where required.
Every dispute is logged with the transaction reference, claimed reason, and channel of receipt, then triaged to a credentialed analyst based on dispute class and Reg E clock urgency.
Analysts assemble evidence from the core banking record, the ticketing system, and policy references before forming a recommendation; at least three independent sources are expected.
Disputes with ambiguous policy application, suspected fraud rings, or amounts above the analyst threshold are escalated to a team lead with a written rationale.
The Reg E ten-business-day and forty-five-day clocks are tracked per case; cases approaching breach are surfaced to the queue owner for same-day action.
Confirmed-error cases are handed to the recovery team with the chargeback reason code, supporting evidence, and the network representment deadline.
Dispute reason codes classify the claim (fraud, authorization, processing error, or consumer dispute) and determine the evidence required to contest a chargeback.
A chargeback may be represented when compelling evidence demonstrates the cardholder participated in the transaction or received the goods or services as described.
Card-network response windows vary by reason code; missing the representment deadline forfeits the right to contest regardless of the strength of the evidence.
Acceptable compelling evidence includes prior undisputed transactions, delivery confirmation, device fingerprints, and signed receipts tied to the cardholder.
Recent credential resets, new device enrollment, and a change of contact details shortly before a disputed transaction are weighted as account-takeover indicators.
Card-not-present disputes require review of the IP geolocation, billing-to-shipping mismatch, and the merchant's fraud-screening response before a liability decision.
Multiple high-value authorizations across distinct merchants within a short window trigger a velocity hold pending customer verification.
Step-up verification is required before releasing provisional credit on suspected first-party fraud, using knowledge-based or one-time-passcode methods.
Access to dispute and customer data is reviewed quarterly; entitlements that no longer match an analyst's role or dispute class are revoked.
Production changes to dispute-handling systems follow documented review, testing, and approval, with the ability to roll back on failure.
Customer information is encrypted in transit and at rest using current industry-standard algorithms, with keys managed in a dedicated key-management service.
Dispute correspondence must state the determination, the consumer's right to documents, and the timeline for any provisional-credit reversal in plain language.
Communications avoid jargon, confirm the disputed amount and date, and provide a single point of contact for follow-up to reduce repeat tickets.
When a claim is denied, the notice explains the basis for the decision and how the consumer may submit additional information for reconsideration.
